title: DDIA 2 · DEFINING NONFUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
subtitle: How fast, how dependable, how it grows, how easy to run and change: each turned into a number.
footer: Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition (Kleppmann & Riccomini). Read the book.

blocks.text: 5,800 posts/s, 200 followers each. Pull = 400M lookups/s; push = ~1M cache writes/s. Celebrities merged at read time.
Response = network + queueing + service time. Queues grow first under load, so measure on the client.
A blip, then timeouts, then retries keep it overloaded. Backoff + jitter, retry budgets, circuit breakers, load shedding.
The user waits for the slowest backend. With 100 backends at 1% slow each, 63% of user requests hit at least one slow call.
A failure is when the whole system stops serving users. You design so faults don't become failures.

items: ~1 in 1,000 machines: a CPU core that miscomputes
config changes: the #1 cause of outages

blocks.text: Software faults are correlated (leap second, the 32,768-hour SSD bug), so replicas do not help. Blameless postmortems fix the process.
Scale up first. Shared-nothing scales furthest but brings all of Part II. Rethink at every 10× of load.

items: Name the load parameter (reads/sec, fan-out, data size), calculate it, then say which component breaks first.
p99 < 200ms for reads, not averages. Mention tail amplification if requests fan out.
Separate fault from failure: "A node dying is a fault. Replicas plus health checks mean it never becomes a failure."

blocks.text: "Before choosing components, let me pin down the load parameters: DAU, read:write ratio, and peak QPS, because they decide whether we need any distribution at all."
